title: Flow matching and rectified flow
summary: Train a network to carry noise to data along straight lines by plain regression, see why the learned paths still curve, how many Euler steps that costs, and how reflow, minibatch OT and SD3 tame it.
outcomes: Explain the conditional flow matching and rectified flow objective and why it needs no ODE simulation in training
Compute interpolated points, target velocities and the averaged marginal velocity at a crossing point
Explain why crossing training lines make learned paths curve and why that raises the number of Euler steps
Compute Euler sampling paths and their error for a given step count
Compare reflow, minibatch OT couplings and SD3's logit-normal timestep sampling as practical fixes

lessons.title: Generating data by following a velocity field from noise

blocks.md:
A generative model has to turn samples from an easy distribution (call it $\pi_0$, usually a standard Gaussian) into samples that look like the data distribution $\pi_1$. Flow models do this with an ordinary differential equation (ODE): start at a noise point $z_0$ and move it for one unit of time with a velocity that depends on where you are and when.

The velocity is a neural network $v_\theta(z, t)$. If it is right, the point lands on something that looks like data at $t = 1$. This course uses the convention of the flow matching and rectified flow papers: $t = 0$ is noise and $t = 1$ is data.

blocks.tex: \frac{dz_t}{dt} = v_\theta(z_t, t), \qquad z_0 \sim \pi_0 = \mathcal{N}(0, I), \qquad z_1 \approx \text{a sample from } \pi_1
blocks.caption: A continuous normalizing flow (CNF): the network only predicts a velocity; an ODE solver turns velocities into a path.

blocks.md:
The old way to train such a model was maximum likelihood, which needs the ODE to be solved (and backpropagated through) on every training step. That is slow, and it is why CNFs stayed small for years.

Flow matching ([Lipman et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747)) and rectified flow ([Liu, Gong and Liu, 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03003)) are *simulation-free*: training is plain regression of $v_\theta$ onto a velocity you can write down in closed form. The ODE is solved only when you sample.

blocks.title: Training is regression; sampling is integration

nodes.label:
Euler steps
z += h v(z, t)

scenes.caption: Training, step 1: draw a noise point, a data point and a random time t, then mix them into a point x_t on the straight line between them. No ODE is solved.
Training, step 2: the network sees only x_t and t and is regressed onto the velocity of that line, x1 - x0. This is ordinary supervised learning with a squared loss.
Sampling: start from fresh noise and repeatedly step along the network's velocity. Only here do we integrate the ODE, and the number of steps sets the cost.

blocks.md:
To see every quantity with real numbers, the course uses a 1D toy problem throughout:

- Source $\pi_0$: standard Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$.
- Target $\pi_1$: two equally likely Gaussian blobs, $\mathcal{N}(-2, 0.5^2)$ and $\mathcal{N}(+2, 0.5^2)$.

In 1D we can compute the best possible velocity field exactly, so the figures show what a perfectly trained network would do. All numbers come from a NumPy script with fixed seeds.
A flow model is a learned velocity field plus an ODE solver. Flow matching makes the *training* of that field as cheap as regression; the *sampling* cost is the number of solver steps.

blocks.question: Why was maximum-likelihood training of continuous normalizing flows expensive compared with flow matching?
options: The loss required simulating the ODE (and backpropagating through it) on every training step
The network had to output a full probability density instead of a velocity
Maximum likelihood cannot be used with Gaussian noise
It needed a discriminator network as in a GAN
blocks.explain: Likelihood training of a CNF integrates the ODE inside the training loop. Flow matching regresses the network onto a closed-form target velocity at a sampled point, so no simulation happens during training.

lessons.title: The training target: straight lines and their velocity

blocks.md:
Pick a noise sample $x_0$ and a data sample $x_1$ independently. Rectified flow joins them with the straight line $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t\,x_1$. Differentiate with respect to $t$ and the velocity along that line is a constant, $x_1 - x_0$.

The network sees a point $x_t$ and the time $t$, and is trained to output that velocity:

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim U[0,1],\; x_0 \sim \pi_0,\; x_1 \sim \pi_1} \big\| (x_1 - x_0) - v_\theta\big((1-t)x_0 + t x_1,\; t\big) \big\|^2
blocks.caption: The rectified flow objective (Liu et al., eq. 1). The same expression is conditional flow matching with straight (optimal transport) conditional paths.

scenes.caption: Four pairs from the toy (seed 0). Columns are t = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. Each row starts at its noise value x0; where it ends depends only on the data point it was randomly paired with.
Halfway: each point is the average of its two endpoints. Pair A started at 0.13 and is heading down; pair B started at -0.13 and is heading up.
At t = 1 every row reaches its data point. The constant step between columns is the velocity divided by 4, because the columns are 0.25 apart.

Bottom row: the regression target of pairs A to D, left to right (not times). Pairs A and B swapped order before t = 0.25 (0.13 vs -0.13, then -0.24 vs 0.52): their lines cross, with targets of opposite sign. Lesson 3 shows why that matters.

blocks.md:
Flow matching arrives at the same recipe from a more general angle. Lipman et al. define a *conditional* probability path $p_t(x \mid x_1)$ that starts as noise and ends concentrated on one data point, with a known velocity $u_t(x \mid x_1)$. The quantity you really want to regress onto is the *marginal* velocity $u_t(x)$ that moves the whole noise distribution to the whole data distribution, but it is an intractable integral over the dataset.

Their key result (Theorem 2): the conditional flow matching loss, which uses the per-sample target $u_t(x \mid x_1)$, has the same gradients as the intractable marginal loss. So regressing onto per-pair targets trains the right field.

blocks.caption: Lipman et al.'s optimal transport (OT) conditional path, a Gaussian whose mean and width change linearly in t. With sigma_min = 0 it is exactly rectified flow's line and target.

blocks.code:
# one training step (PyTorch-style), t=0 noise, t=1 data
x1 = next(data_iter)                    # batch of data, shape (B, D)
x0 = torch.randn_like(x1)               # independent Gaussian noise
t  = torch.rand(x1.shape[0], 1)         # t ~ U[0, 1], one per sample
xt = (1 - t) * x0 + t * x1              # point on the straight line
target = x1 - x0                        # velocity of that line
loss = ((model(xt, t) - target) ** 2).mean()
opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
blocks.caption: The whole training loop. No ODE solver appears anywhere.

blocks.md: The training loss does not go to zero even for a perfect network. Different pairs pass through the same $(x_t, t)$ with different targets, and a regression can only output their average. That average is the field you want, as lesson 3 shows.

blocks.question: A pair has $x_0 = 0.1$ and $x_1 = 1.37$. At $t = 0.75$, what input does the network get and what target is it regressed onto?
options: Input 1.37, target 1.27
Input 1.05, target 0.32 (the distance still to go)
Input 0.1, target 1.37
Input 1.05, target 1.27
blocks.explain: $x_{0.75} = 0.25 \cdot 0.1 + 0.75 \cdot 1.37 = 1.05$ (pair D in the figure) and the target velocity is constant along the line: $1.37 - 0.1 = 1.27$. The target does not shrink with t; it is a velocity, not a remaining distance.

blocks.question: Which statement about conditional flow matching is correct?
options: It needs the marginal velocity field computed over the whole dataset at every step
It only works with straight-line paths
Regressing onto per-sample conditional velocities gives the same gradient as regressing onto the intractable marginal velocity
It trains by maximizing the log-likelihood of the data under the ODE
blocks.explain: Lipman et al. Theorem 2: the CFM and FM losses differ by a constant independent of the parameters, so their gradients match. Straight OT paths are one choice; diffusion-style Gaussian paths also fit the framework.

lessons.title: Crossing lines and why the learned paths curve

blocks.md:
Take two training pairs whose lines cross: pair P goes from $x_0 = -1$ to $x_1 = +2$ and pair Q from $x_0 = +1$ to $x_1 = -2$. Both lines pass through $x = 0$ at $t = 1/3$, with velocities $+3$ and $-3$.

An ODE cannot follow both: at a given point and time it has exactly one velocity. So what does the trained network output there?

blocks.prompt: In the toy, by symmetry, pairs heading to the +2 blob and to the -2 blob pass through $(x = 0, t = 1/3)$ equally often. What velocity does the loss-minimizing network output at that point?
blocks.reveal: **Zero.** The squared loss is minimized by the conditional mean of the targets, $v^*(x,t) = \mathbb{E}[x_1 - x_0 \mid x_t = x]$ (Liu et al., eq. 2). At the symmetric crossing point the upward and downward targets cancel. The learned flow does not pick one line; it averages them, and the averaged paths are no longer straight.

blocks.tex: v^*(x, t) = \mathbb{E}\big[x_1 - x_0 \,\big|\, x_t = x\big] = \sum_k P(k \mid x_t = x)\,\mathbb{E}[x_1 - x_0 \mid x_t = x, k]
blocks.caption: The marginal velocity, split over the two blobs k. In the toy both factors have closed forms, which is how the figures are computed.

blocks.title: Velocity targets versus the learned average

scenes.caption: At x = 0, t = 1/3: the expected target for pairs heading to the +2 blob is +2.82, for the -2 blob -2.82. Each is equally likely here (posterior 0.50), so v* = 0.
At x = 0.5, t = 0.5: pairs heading up have mean target 2.60, pairs heading down -3.80. But 96.1 percent of the pairs passing here are heading up, so v* = 2.35.

blocks.title: The exact marginal velocity field of the toy

scenes.caption: Early (t = 0.05): almost nothing is known about where a point is going, so v* is close to -x, pulling every point toward 0, the average of the two blobs.
At t = 1/3 the field starts to commit: near 0 it is still a blend of the two blob targets, but further out it follows one of them.
At t = 0.5 the switch near x = 0 is steep: a point slightly above 0 is almost surely heading up, slightly below heading down. Paths that drifted to the middle now bend sharply.
Late (t = 0.9) v* follows one target almost everywhere. The path of a single point is therefore curved: first toward the middle, then out to a blob. Drag t to explore.

blocks.md:
This is the rectified flow paper's *non-crossing* picture. Paths of a well-defined ODE cannot cross, so the learned flow *rewires* crossing straight lines at their intersections, while keeping the same distribution at every time (Liu et al., Theorem 3.3, the marginal preserving property).

In 1D the consequence is stark: the flow preserves order, so a noise sample at 0.5 must end at the matching quantile of the target, about 1.85, no matter which data point it was paired with during training.

Straight training targets do not mean straight sampling paths. Each conditional path is a line, but the marginal flow, which is what the network learns and what sampling follows, curves wherever many lines cross.

blocks.question: You train a rectified flow on a dataset with many well-separated modes. Training loss plateaus well above zero even with a huge network. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The learning rate is too high
Many line pairs with different targets pass through the same (x_t, t), so the irreducible error of the conditional mean remains
The network is underfitting because the target x1 - x0 changes along each line
The time t should be sampled from noise to data in reverse
blocks.explain: The optimal predictor is the conditional mean of the targets; their spread around that mean is irreducible. The target is constant along each line, so it is not a moving target.

lessons.title: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps

blocks.md:
To sample, integrate the learned ODE from $t=0$ to $t=1$. The simplest solver is Euler: with $N$ steps of size $h = 1/N$, repeat $z \leftarrow z + h\,v_\theta(z, t)$. Each step is one network call, so $N$ is the number of function evaluations (NFE), the main cost of generation.

Euler assumes the velocity stays fixed for a whole step. On a straight path at constant speed that is exact; on a curved path it overshoots or undershoots.

blocks.caption: Euler sampler. Higher-order solvers (Heun, RK4, adaptive) spend more calls per step for less error.

blocks.prompt: Start the toy at $z_0 = 0.5$ and take a single Euler step with the exact field $v^*$. Where does it land? (Hint: at $t = 0$, $v^*(x, 0) = -x$.)
blocks.reveal: At **0**, exactly between the blobs: $0.5 + 1 \cdot (-0.5) = 0$. At $t=0$ the field points toward the *mean* of the data, because nothing yet distinguishes where a point is going. One step of a curved flow produces the average of the data, which for images looks like a blur. The correct endpoint is about 1.85.

blocks.title: Euler paths from z0 = 0.5 versus the exact flow

scenes.caption: The exact flow (fine RK4 solve, drawn through samples every 0.1) dips toward the middle and then curves up to 1.85. Simplified: the field is the exact optimum, standing in for a trained network.
One Euler step follows the initial velocity -0.5 for the whole interval and lands at 0: error 1.85.
Two steps: the second step starts at t = 0.5 from 0.25, where v* = 1.82, and lands at 1.16. Error 0.69.
Four steps track the bend much better and land at 1.58. Error 0.27. The remaining gap comes from the sharp turn between about t = 0.2 and 0.5.

blocks.title: Endpoint error versus number of Euler steps

scenes.caption: Error of the single path from z0 = 0.5. Beyond 4 steps the error roughly halves each time the steps double, the first-order behavior expected from Euler.
Mean error over 4000 noise samples (seed 1), measured against each sample's exact endpoint. Same pattern: 1 step is useless, 16 steps is within 0.09.

blocks.md: Real models show the same tradeoff. Lipman et al. report that on ImageNet 32x32 their flow matching model with OT paths needed roughly 60 percent of the function evaluations of diffusion-path models to reach the same numerical error with fixed-step solvers. Liu et al. show that a first rectified flow already gives good images with very few Euler steps, and lesson 5 is about making it work with one.
Sampling cost is set by how curved the learned paths are. A perfectly straight, constant-speed flow is solved exactly by one Euler step.

blocks.question: A flow model gives sharp images at 50 Euler steps but blurry, averaged-looking images at 1 step. Which change most directly attacks the cause?
options: Train longer with the same objective
Use a larger batch size
Make the learned paths straighter, for example with reflow or an OT-based coupling
Lower the learning rate at the end of training
blocks.explain: A single step follows the initial velocity, which points toward the data mean wherever paths are curved. Training the same objective better converges to the same curved field; straightening the paths is what lets few steps work.

blocks.question: Doubling Euler steps from 8 to 16 on the toy cut the endpoint error from about 0.135 to about 0.067. What does that ratio indicate?
options: Error is roughly proportional to step size, so Euler is first order
Euler is a second-order method
The flow is straight
The network is overfitting
blocks.explain: Halving h roughly halved the error, which is first-order behavior: global error proportional to h. A second-order method like Heun would cut it by about 4x.

lessons.title: Reflow and OT couplings: making the paths straight

blocks.md:
The paths curve because noise and data were paired at random, so lines cross. Rectified flow's fix is *reflow*: after training the first flow (1-rectified flow), use it to generate new pairs. Draw noise $z_0$, run the ODE to get $z_1$, and train a second flow on the pairs $(z_0, z_1)$ with the same straight-line loss.

The paths of an ODE flow never cross (lesson 3), so the straight lines between its start and end points cross far less often (in 1D, never), the new training lines barely conflict and the new flow, the 2-rectified flow, follows them almost exactly.

blocks.caption: Liu et al., Algorithm 1. Each reflow trains on the input and output pairs of the previous flow.

blocks.title: Re-pairing the four seeded noise samples

scenes.caption: Original random pairing (lesson 2). Mean squared transport cost over these four pairs: 2.89. Several lines cross (A with B and D, B with C and D).
Reflow: each noise value is paired with where the 1-rectified flow sends it (in 1D, the matching quantile of the target). Order is preserved and the cost drops to 1.57.
Minibatch OT (Tong et al.) instead re-pairs within the batch to minimize squared distance; in 1D that is sorting both lists. Cost 2.19, no crossings, and no ODE needed.

blocks.title: After reflow, one Euler step is enough

scenes.caption: Before reflow: the 1-rectified flow from z0 = 0.5 curves, and one Euler step lands at 0.
After reflow the pair (0.5, 1.85) is trained as a straight line with constant velocity 1.35. One Euler step lands exactly on 1.85. Simplified: a real reflowed network is only nearly straight.

blocks.md:
Two guarantees from the rectified flow paper make this sound:

- **Marginals are preserved** (Theorem 3.3): the new pairs are still a valid coupling of noise and data.
- **Transport cost does not increase** for any convex cost (Theorem 3.5). In the toy, over 200,000 samples, the mean squared distance $\mathbb{E}\|x_1 - x_0\|^2$ drops from 5.25 (random pairs) to 1.48 (reflowed pairs).

Repeated reflow provably drives a straightness measure toward zero. In practice one reflow already makes paths nearly straight; Liu et al. then distilled the 2-rectified flow into a one-step model and report a one-step CIFAR-10 FID of 4.85.

Reflow costs a full extra training run plus generating many pairs with the first model, and errors in the first flow are baked into the second. [Tong et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.00482) offer a cheaper route, OT-CFM: inside each training minibatch, solve a small optimal transport problem between the noise and data samples and train on those pairs. With independent pairs (their I-CFM, equivalent to rectified flow when the path has no noise) paths cross; with minibatch OT they cross less, giving straighter flows and faster inference. The batch only approximates the global OT plan.

blocks.question: Why does training a new flow on pairs $(z_0, z_1)$ generated by the first flow give straighter paths than training on random pairs?
options: The generated z1 are higher quality than real data
Reflow uses a smaller learning rate
Reflow switches to a second-order ODE solver
The lines between generated pairs cross far less often, so the conditional-mean averaging that bends paths largely disappears
blocks.explain: ODE trajectories cannot cross, so the coupling they define is largely untangled. With few crossings, each point (x_t, t) is reached by essentially one line, its target is unambiguous, and the learned field matches that straight line.

blocks.question: A team has a large text-to-image flow model and a tight compute budget. Which is the main cost they accept if they choose reflow over minibatch OT-CFM?
options: Reflow changes the data distribution the model generates
Reflow requires simulating the first model to generate many training pairs and then a second training run
Reflow cannot be combined with Euler sampling
Reflow increases transport cost
blocks.explain: Reflow preserves marginals and does not increase convex transport costs, but each round needs a trained model, a large batch of ODE simulations to create pairs, and another training run. Minibatch OT only re-pairs samples inside each training batch.

lessons.title: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3

blocks.md:
Diffusion models such as DDPM ([Ho et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239)) also move between data and Gaussian noise, using a Gaussian path $x_t = a_t x + b_t \epsilon$ with curved schedules, and train a network to predict the noise $\epsilon$. [Song et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456) showed that the stochastic reverse process has a deterministic *probability flow ODE* with the same marginal distributions, so a diffusion model can also be sampled as an ODE.

Flow matching places these in one family. Lipman et al. show that the variance exploding (noise is added with growing variance) and variance preserving (the signal is shrunk as noise is added, keeping total variance fixed) diffusion paths are particular Gaussian conditional paths, while the OT path is the straight one. Their diffusion-path trajectories can overshoot and backtrack; the OT trajectories stay straight.

[Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden's stochastic interpolants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15571), developed at the same time, take the same view: pick any time-dependent interpolation between two densities, learn the velocity with a simple quadratic loss, and skip the diffusion SDE entirely. Flow matching, rectified flow and stochastic interpolants are three routes to essentially the same simulation-free recipe.

[Stable Diffusion 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03206) (Esser et al., 2024) trains a large text-to-image transformer with the rectified flow objective. Note the flipped time convention: SD3 writes $z_t = (1-t)x_0 + t\epsilon$, so $t=0$ is data and $t=1$ is noise, and the velocity target is $\epsilon - x_0$.

Their main training change is *where* in time to spend the loss. Predicting the velocity is trivial near both ends and hardest in the middle, so instead of $t \sim U[0,1]$ they sample $t$ from a logit-normal distribution: draw $u \sim \mathcal{N}(m, s^2)$ and set $t = 1/(1+e^{-u})$.

scenes.caption: rf/lognorm(0.00, 1.00), the setting that ranked best overall in SD3's comparison. Peak density 1.60 at t = 0.5; only about 1.4 percent of samples fall in each of the last tenths near 0 and 1.
Positive m shifts training toward the noise end (here m = 1, s = 0.6, peak near t = 0.77). The paper's ablation ranked it second overall, behind rf/lognorm(0.00, 1.00).
Negative m shifts training toward the data end. Use the sliders: the density always vanishes at both endpoints, which is why the paper also tested a heavy-tailed mode sampler.

blocks.md:
SD3's ablation (61 formulations across two datasets and many sampler settings) found:

- Rectified flow with logit-normal timesteps, rf/lognorm(0.00, 1.00), consistently ranked well and beat plain rectified flow with uniform timesteps.
- Rectified flow formulations held up better than other formulations when sampling with fewer steps.
- At 1024x1024 they shift timesteps toward more noise, because more pixels need more noise to destroy the signal; they used a shift of 3.0 during training and sampling at that resolution.

When reading code or papers, check the time convention before the sign of anything. Rectified flow and flow matching papers use noise at $t=0$ and target $x_1 - x_0$; SD3 and its descendants use data at $t=0$ and target $\epsilon - x_0$. The math is the same with $t$ replaced by $1 - t$.

blocks.question: Why does SD3 sample training timesteps from a logit-normal instead of uniformly?
options: The velocity regression is easiest near t = 0 and t = 1, so spending more training samples on intermediate t gives a better model
Uniform sampling makes the ODE solver unstable at test time
Logit-normal sampling removes the need for classifier-free guidance
It makes the paths straight without reflow
blocks.explain: Esser et al. argue that near the ends the target is easy to predict (close to pure data or pure noise), and confirm experimentally that rf/lognorm(0.00, 1.00) beats uniform rectified flow. It reweights the loss over time; it does not change the paths or the sampler.

blocks.question: Your codebase follows SD3: $z_t = (1-t)x_0 + t\epsilon$ with $x_0$ data. A colleague plugs in a rectified flow sampler that starts at $t=0$ from noise and adds $h \cdot v$. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, the conventions are identical
Only the step size needs to double
It starts from noise at the data end of time and steps in the wrong direction; it must start at t = 1 and integrate toward t = 0 (subtracting h times the predicted velocity)
It works but needs logit-normal sampling at inference
blocks.explain: Under SD3's convention noise lives at t = 1 and the network predicts the velocity toward noise, epsilon - x0. Sampling must run t from 1 down to 0, i.e. z goes to z - h v. Mixing conventions silently produces garbage.

blocks.question: Which statement best describes the relation between diffusion models and flow matching?
options: They are unrelated; diffusion requires an SDE and cannot be sampled with an ODE
Diffusion paths are Gaussian conditional paths within the flow matching framework, and diffusion models can be sampled with the probability flow ODE
Flow matching is a special case of DDPM with a different noise schedule
Flow matching can only learn straight paths, diffusion can learn curved ones
blocks.explain: Lipman et al. recover VE and VP diffusion paths as Gaussian conditional paths, and Song et al.'s probability flow ODE gives diffusion models a deterministic sampler. The marginal flow of any of these, including OT paths, can be curved.
